title: How to See the Partial Lunar Eclipse and Blood Moon on August 27
gist: A science explainer on the partial lunar eclipse and 'blood moon' visible the night of August 27, 2026, covering eclipse mechanics and viewing tips, with no technology-investor relevance.

insights.claim: A partial lunar eclipse producing a reddish 'blood moon' occurred the night of August 27 into early August 28, 2026, reaching a magnitude of 0.93 (about 93 percent of the moon's diameter in Earth's darkest shadow), lasting roughly 3 hours and 18 minutes, with the Americas as the best viewing region.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: A purely astronomical/consumer-interest event with no technology-sector or investor relevance.

insights.claim: The reddish 'blood moon' color occurs because Earth's atmosphere filters out blue wavelengths of sunlight during the eclipse, leaving red-spectrum light to illuminate the moon, described by NASA as projecting the world's sunrises and sunsets onto the lunar surface.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Explains the underlying physical mechanism of the phenomenon for reader understanding; not investor-relevant.
insights.quote: It's as if all of the world's sunrises and sunsets are projected onto the moon.
insights.locator: section on what causes a blood moon

insights.claim: Unlike solar eclipses, no eye protection is needed to view a lunar eclipse directly; the article recommends viewing from areas free of light pollution, using binoculars or a telescope if available, and also observing the surrounding night sky as stars become more visible while the moon dims.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Practical consumer viewing guidance with no bearing on markets or technology investment themes.
insights.locator: section on how to best view a lunar eclipse
